endorsements.title: Adoption of AI in Healthcare Delivery Systems: Early Applications and Impacts
endorsements.quote: Additional research is required to understand clinician experience with ambient scribe, particularly in identifying which visit types are most suited to its use.

endorsements.title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement
endorsements.issuer: ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR, RSNA; Radiol Artif Intell 2024 (PMID 38251899, doi:10.1148/ryai.230513)
endorsements.quote: Hence, some AI models may be deployed on a subset of exams because disease prevalence in that exam subset is increased from baseline.

endorsements.title: [Proposal for Responsible Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Medical Practice]
endorsements.quote: Un posicionamiento importante, desde el punto de vista asistencial, es priorizar la aplicación de la IA generativa en la reducción de las tareas administrativas y repetitivas de bajo valor clínico.

endorsements.title: Conference Report: The FutuRE oF MinimalLy InvasivE GI and Capsule DiagnosTics (REFLECT), September 2025
endorsements.quote: CE is most valuable when applied selectively, not universally.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Mediated Teledentistry for Ageing Populations: Toward Intelligent Intermediary Support in Home-Based Oral Care
endorsements.quote: Initial deployment may focus on high-yield applications such as postoperative follow-up, preventive monitoring in dependent older adults, triage of urgent complaints, and caregiver-supported oral hygiene supervision.

evidence.title: From Concept to Clinic: Real World Evidence for Autonomous AI Deployment in Primary Care Telemedicine
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic agreement in confidence-gated, common, lower-complexity encounters
evidence.effect: Top-1 diagnostic agreement was 91.3% overall, 96.3% among confidence-threshold-eligible cases, and 97.9% among common, lower-complexity conditions meeting the same threshold.
evidence.quote: The AI’s top-1 diagnosis matched the clinician’s diagnosis in 91.3% of cases overall, increasing to 96.3% among cases meeting a pre-specified safety confidence threshold, and 97.9% in common, lower-complexity conditions that met the same confidence threshold.

evidence.title: Comparative cost analysis of community-based tuberculosis screening: Computer-Aided Detection (CAD) alone versus CAD with point-of-care C-reactive protein testing in South Africa and Lesotho
evidence.outcome: Modelled cost per TB case detected at higher prevalence
evidence.effect: At modelled 1% TB prevalence with participant numbers and total costs held constant, cost per case decreased from USD 5,454 to USD 2,887 (CAD4TBv7) and USD 7,486 to USD 3,975 (CAD4TBv7-CRP).
evidence.quote: However, the average cost per TB case detected decreased substantially to USD 2,887 (95% UI: USD 2,272–3,587) for the CAD4TBv7 approach and USD 3,975 (95% UI: USD 3,157-4,907) for the CAD4TBv7-CRP approach ( Table 2 ) when compared with the primary analysis.

evidence.title: Large Language Model–Assisted Radiology Reporting: A Retrospective Cohort Study Using the UTAUT Framework to Analyze Workflow Integration and Efficiency Gains
evidence.outcome: Inter-study interval time by modality, comparing baseline vs LLM-assisted periods
evidence.effect: Reductions for outpatient CT with contrast (23.0 vs 13.0 min; p=0.0021) and without contrast (18.5 vs 7.0 min; p=0.0017); no improvement for MRI with contrast (14.0 vs 16.0; p=0.2808) or without contrast (14.0 vs 7.0; p=0.0889).
evidence.quote: LLM assistance significantly reduced inter-study intervals for outpatient CT with contrast (23.0 vs 13.0 minutes; difference 10 minutes; p = 0.0021) and without contrast (18.5 vs 7.0 minutes; difference 11.5 minutes; p = 0.0017).
evidence.sample_unit: radiology studies (CT and MRI) interpreted by a single radiologist

evidence.title: Implementation costs and cost-effectiveness of ultraportable chest X-ray with artificial intelligence in active case finding for tuberculosis in Nigeria
evidence.outcome: cost per case at varied prevalence
evidence.effect: AI screening had a lower cost per case detected than any-symptom screening only when the proportion of asymptomatic TB exceeded 30%.
evidence.quote: Our analysis showed that using CXR and AI had lower cost per case detected than any symptom screening criteria when asymptomatic TB was higher than 30% of all bacteriologically-confirmed TB detected.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence-generated encounter summaries: early insights from ambulatory clinicians at a large academic health system
evidence.outcome: Change in EHR clinical review time per visit by baseline review time
evidence.effect: Average review time fell from 3:22 to 3:04 minutes per visit. Each extra minute of baseline review time was linked to an 8.6-second larger reduction (P = .046).
evidence.quote: Higher baseline review time was significantly associated with greater post-implementation reductions, with each additional minute at baseline linked to an 8.6-second decrease in review time (P = .046).
evidence.sample_unit: providers with complete Epic Signal time data

evidence.title: Subjective and objective impacts of ambulatory AI scribes
evidence.venue: The American journal of managed care
evidence.outcome: Whether baseline documentation time modifies DocTime reduction from AI scribe use
evidence.effect: Each additional 10% of encounters with scribe use cut DocTime by just over 30 seconds per scheduled hour (P<.001); less-efficient physicians with higher baseline DocTime realized most savings.
evidence.quote: This effect was modified by baseline DocTime, with less-efficient physicians realizing the majority of time savings.

evidence.title: TARGET-AI  : a foundational approach for the targeted deployment of artificial intelligence electrocardiography in the electronic health record
evidence.outcome: F1 score and false positives for targeted vs untargeted AI-ECG screening across SHD labels
evidence.effect: Targeted screening in temporal validation (n=5,198) significantly increased F1 (median 0.25 [0.09 to 0.75]) and decreased false positives (median -303 [-715 to -77]) across 26 SHD labels.
evidence.quote: Compared with untargeted AI-ECG screening, targeted screening in the temporal validation set (n=5,198) was associated with a significant increase in F1 scores (median of 0.25 [range: 0.09 to 0.75]) and decrease in false positives (median of –303 [range: –715 to –77]) across 26 SHD labels.
evidence.sample_unit: individuals referred for first TTE (temporal validation); also 33,518 UK Biobank participants and 3,628 MIMIC-IV patients

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence-driven streamlining of prostate cancer multidisciplinary team recommendations in a tertiary NHS centre in the UK
evidence.outcome: Concordance with MDT recommendations in a targeted subset versus all evaluable cases
evidence.effect: A machine learning-derived decision tree identified 93 patients for streamlined management with 97.8% concordance, compared with 85.6% concordance across all 355 evaluable cases in phase two.
evidence.quote: Notably, using a machine learning-derived decision tree enabled the identification of 93 patients for streamlined management, demonstrating a 97.8% concordance in this subgroup (P < 0.01).

evidence.title: Risk-Guided Atrial Fibrillation Screening With Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Electrocardiogram Models: A VITAL-AF Trial Analysis
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
evidence.outcome: AF screening effect (incident AF diagnosis rate difference) across AI risk deciles
evidence.effect: Screening effect seen only in top CH-AI decile: 10.07 vs 7.76/100 person-years, difference 2.32 (95% CI 0.01-4.63), number-needed-to-screen 43 per year; trade-off with reduced population coverage.
evidence.quote: An AF screening effect was observed in the top decile of CH-AI (AF diagnosis rate in screening 10.07/100 person-years [95% 8.28-11.87] vs 7.76 [95% 6.30-9.21] in control, P < 0.05), corresponding to a difference in AF diagnosis rate of 2.32/100 person-years (95% CI: 0.01-4.63) and number-needed-to-screen of 43 per year.

evidence.title: Effects of Implementing Artificial Intelligence-Based Computer-Aided Detection for Chest Radiographs in Daily Practice on the Rate of Referral to Chest Computed Tomography in Pulmonology Outpatient Clinic
evidence.outcome: Chest CT referral rate, including referrals with negative CT results, with versus without AI-CAD
evidence.effect: AI-CAD use was associated with increased chest CT referrals (OR 1.33; P=0.008) and referrals with negative CT results (OR 1.46; P=0.005). Referrals with positive CT results were not significantly changed (OR 1.08; P=0.647).
evidence.quote: The use of AI-CAD for CR interpretation in pulmonology outpatients was independently associated with an increased frequency of overall referrals for chest CT scans and referrals with subsequent negative results.

evidence.title: Deep Learning to Detect Intracranial Hemorrhage in a National Teleradiology Program and the Impact on Interpretation Time
evidence.outcome: AI performance and read time in high-volume, low-prevalence teleradiology setting
evidence.effect: Prevalence 2.70%, PPV 21.1%; falsely flagged exams took mean 9:40 vs 8:25 pre-AI and 8:38 post-AI unflagged (P<.001), so inefficiencies may outweigh benefits.
evidence.quote: With lengthened read times for falsely flagged examinations, system inefficiencies may outweigh the potential benefits of using the tool in a high volume, low prevalence environment.

evidence.title: An AI-Powered Strategy for Managing Patient Messaging Load and Reducing Burnout
evidence.outcome: Draft utilization and time savings by role and specialty
evidence.effect: Overall draft utilization 38%; clinicians 43% vs scheduling staff 33%. Time saved 23 seconds for support staff vs 3 seconds for clinicians; variability across specialties.
evidence.quote: However, the effectiveness of artificial intelligence (AI)-generated draft responses varies by clinical role and specialty, indicating the need for tailored implementations.

evidence.title: CATalyze-AI: accelerating referral for thrombectomy in acute stroke patients using an AI-based software. A prospective, multicentre, quasi-experimental cohort study
evidence.outcome: Real-world positive predictive value of AI LVO detection across the tele-stroke population
evidence.effect: Among transferred patients, NCCT high-probability predictions had 66% (41/62) EVT and CTA 67% (36/54). Screening-log estimates across all scans suggested modest-to-weak real-world PPV.
evidence.quote: These estimations suggested a modest-to-weak real-world performance and support the concept that AI-based LVO detection tools are most appropriately applied in clinically pre-selected populations with moderate-to-high suspicion of LVO.

evidence.title: Prospective Shadow-Mode Evaluation of an Artificial Intelligence Tool for Intracranial Aneurysm Detection on CT Angiography: Incremental Yield and Operational Impact
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
evidence.outcome: Operational yield metrics (rEDR, gain-to-pain ratio, NNE) by care setting
evidence.effect: Favorable in inpatients (rEDR 78.3%, GPR 2.57, NNE 28.9) and emergency (rEDR 37.1%, GPR 1.0, NNE 85.3); unfavorable in outpatients (rEDR 14.1%, GPR 0.67, NNE 130.3).
evidence.quote: Operational metrics were most favorable in inpatients (rEDR 78.3%, GPR 2.57, NNE 28.9) and emergency (rEDR 37.1%, GPR 1.0, NNE 85.3) and were unfavorable in outpatients (rEDR 14.1%, GPR 0.67, NNE 130.3).

evidence.title: Utilization of Generative AI-drafted Responses for Managing Patient-Provider Communication
evidence.outcome: Share of AI drafts generated for messages that received no response
evidence.effect: Drafts generated for all messages, including 80% that received no response, adding review burden; overall utilization low at 19.4%.
evidence.quote: GenAI drafts were generated for all messages, including 80% that received no response, adding to the review burden and potentially undermining efficiency.

evidence.title: Long-term impact of artificial intelligence on colorectal adenoma detection in high-risk colonoscopy
evidence.outcome: Adenoma detection rate before vs after AI in high-risk diagnostic colonoscopy
evidence.effect: ADR 38.1% pre-AI vs 42.0% early (P=0.77), 40.0% established (P=0.44), 39.5% late (P=0.77); no significant differences in PDR, advanced ADR, or non-neoplastic PDR.
evidence.quote: In patients with an increased pre-test probability of having an abnormal colonoscopy, the current generation of AI did not yield enhanced CRC screening metrics over high-quality colonoscopy.

evidence.title: Enhancing Diagnostic Accuracy of Lung Nodules in Chest Computed Tomography Using Artificial Intelligence: Retrospective Analysis
evidence.outcome: False positive and false negative rates of lung nodule detection before vs after AI implementation
evidence.effect: At Hospital A, false negative rate fell from 8.4% to 5.16% while false positive rate rose from 2.36% to 9.77% (P<.001); accuracy fell from 93.33% to 92.23% (A) and 95.27% to 92.77% (C).
evidence.quote: At Hospital A, the false negative rate decreased from 8.4% to 5.16% (χ<sup>2</sup><sub>1</sub>=9.85; P=.002), while the false positive rate increased from 2.36% to 9.77% (χ<sup>2</sup><sub>1</sub>=53.48; P<.001).

evidence.title: Evaluating the performance of artificial intelligence software for lung nodule detection on chest radiographs in a retrospective real-world UK population
evidence.outcome: Low PPV in low-prevalence population causing false positives and over-investigation
evidence.effect: PPV 5.5% with 1.6% cancer prevalence; 943 false positives; low PPV risks over-investigation and limits clinical translation.
evidence.quote: The low PPV carries the risk of over-investigation and limits the translation of the software to clinical practice.

evidence.title: Head-to-Head Comparison of 2 Artificial Intelligence Tools for Detecting Lymph Node Metastases in Whole-Slide Pathology Images Within and Beyond Their Intended Use
evidence.venue: Modern pathology : an official journal of the United States and Canadian Academy of Pathology, Inc
evidence.outcome: False-positive alert rates in tumor-negative slides
evidence.effect: FPA rates were substantial for both tools; VMD generally produced more alerts, especially in lung and breast cancer. High FPA rates, even in lung cancer within DPL's intended use, may limit practical use.
evidence.quote: FPA rates were substantial for both tools, with VMD generally producing more alerts, especially in lung and breast cancer.
evidence.sample_unit: patients with lymph node metastases (whole-slide images); plus 1012 tumor-negative slides for false-positive alerts

evidence.title: AI-Powered Chest X-Ray for Diagnosing Pulmonary Tuberculosis in County and Township Health Care Facilities in Yichang: Retrospective, Real-World Study
evidence.outcome: CAD false positives and positive rate in low-prevalence symptomatic population
evidence.effect: CAD flagged 13,515 (14.5%) as positive with PPV 1.7% at 0.3% prevalence, versus radiologist positive rate 0.7%.
evidence.quote: However, excessive reliance on CAD-based diagnoses may potentially contribute to a higher volume of unnecessary follow-up procedures, leading to an inefficient allocation of medical resources.

commentary.bottom_line: Nine studies, mostly pre-post or simulated designs, consistently suggest that limiting AI to higher-prevalence exams, confidence-gated cases, or high-burden clinicians improves yield, cost per case, or time savings. No study randomized targeted against broad deployment in routine care or measured outcomes for patients left outside the eligible subset.

perspectives.view: Nine studies test targeting, and all report findings favoring it. None randomizes targeted versus broad deployment in routine care. The one cluster trial is an offline analysis, and five studies use pre-post or simulated designs. Findings point the same way across radiology, TB, cardiology, and scribes. Risk of bias and indirectness lower certainty to low.

In a simulated replay, targeted AI-ECG screening cut false positives by a median of 303 across 26 labels. A decision tree reached 97.8% concordance with multidisciplinary team plans in 93 selected patients versus 85.6% across 355 cases. Confidence-gated encounters showed 96.3% diagnostic agreement versus 91.3% for all encounters. Harm outside the subset went unmeasured.

Each additional 10% of encounters with scribe use cut documentation time by about 30 seconds per scheduled hour, and physicians with higher baseline time gained most. Each extra baseline minute of chart review predicted an 8.6-second larger reduction. LLM assistance shortened CT but not MRI intervals for one radiologist, which suggests benefit varies by exam type.

At a modelled 1% TB prevalence, cost per case detected fell from USD 5,454 to USD 2,887 for CAD4TBv7. In Nigeria, AI screening cost less per case than symptom screening only when asymptomatic TB exceeded 30%. These results suggest value depends on local prevalence, which systems would need to estimate before choosing deployment sites.

Two TB studies included rural and low-literacy populations in southern Africa and Nigeria. No test enrolled US Medicaid, safety-net, or limited English proficiency patients. No study examined which patient groups fall outside eligibility rules built on prevalence, model confidence, or documentation burden.

In the atrial fibrillation cluster trial, screening raised diagnoses only in the top AI risk decile (10.07 vs 7.76 per 100 person-years; number needed to screen 43 per year), and the authors report reduced population coverage. Patients outside a targeted subset may lose access to screening, and no study reported how those patients fared.

commentary.research_gap: No study randomized patients, clinicians, or sites to targeted versus broad AI deployment in real care, and none tracked missed diagnoses, delays, or access among patients excluded by eligibility rules. Trials in US safety-net and Medicaid settings that report both yield inside the subset and outcomes outside it would address the main uncertainty.
commentary.underserved_note: Two tests included underserved groups: rural participants in South Africa and Lesotho, and a low-health-literacy population in Nigeria, both in TB screening. No test included US Medicaid, safety-net, or limited English proficiency patients. Findings on targeting scribes, radiology tools, or cardiac screening therefore may not transfer to those populations, and eligibility rules could exclude them without anyone detecting it.
